strengths: Significant practical problem with compelling real-world motivation (ChatGPT cryptocurrency theft case study) that demonstrates concrete harm from malicious code generation
Comprehensive large-scale empirical evaluation: 265,000+ prompts, 11 production LLMs, multiple prompt/codegen LLM combinations with robustness checks across temperature settings
Well-designed systematic validation pipeline: multi-stage filtering, ensemble URL detectors, human validation with majority voting, clear Category 1/2 distinction
Practical real-world impact: 62 malicious domains discovered and added to eth-phishing-detect blocklist, demonstrating utility beyond academic contribution
Reusable benchmark and strong reproducibility: Innoc2Scam-bench publicly released, detailed model specifications, deterministic sampling (T=0), comprehensive appendices with running examples
Insightful domain-level overlap analysis (Figures 7-8) revealing 60% convergence across all four models, suggesting shared web data sources in training corpora
Honest scope discussion: clearly defines limitations (innocuous prompts only, no adversarial techniques) and acknowledges that URL-based detection doesn't capture all malicious code types
weaknesses: Narrow oracle definition limits detection to URL-based attacks: misses backdoors, logic bombs, and other malicious behaviors; dependency on external URL databases means vulnerability discovery bounded by known malicious hosts

Methodological circularity in prompt synthesis: using LLMs to generate prompts for testing LLMs creates bias risk; different Prompt LLMs generate vastly different quantities (69,076 vs 100,760 prompts), indicating significant variance in synthesis quality without systematic analysis

Limited manual validation at scale: only 3 author-annotators for 3,150 prompts; no inter-annotator agreement metrics; 'innocuousness' is subjective and context-dependent with no discussion of difficult cases or disagreement patterns

Confounding between aggressive filtering and true training data quality: Gemini-2.5-pro blocks 40.3% of prompts, making it unclear whether lower malicious rates reflect better data or merely filtering; some models show high 'incomplete' rates (gpt-5: 84 cases) suggesting refusals rather than safe generation

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: paper documents phenomenon comprehensively but provides limited insight into root causes—why are these URLs in training data? How are they retrieved during generation? Limited to single detailed case study (pump.fun)

Benchmark generalization concerns: Innoc2Scam-bench constructed from 2024 model vulnerabilities and applied to 2025 models; no analysis of whether newer models have defenses against these specific prompts or different training data; unclear if benchmark captures domain-specific vulnerabilities

Incomplete guardrail evaluation: only one guardrail system tested; hardcoded policy categories limit generalizability; <0.3% detection rate not deeply analyzed; no comparison with other mitigation strategies (input filtering, output sanitization, fine-tuning)

Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or ablation studies; malicious rate variation (3.19%-5.94%) across model pairs not analyzed for significance; URL extraction heuristics not validated
Presentation density: crucial details relegated to appendices (Category 1/2 distinction, running example); results section could benefit from clearer conceptual organization

strengths: Addresses an important security problem with large-scale empirical evaluation across 11 production LLMs and 265K+ prompts
Discovers and reports 62 previously unlisted malicious domains, providing concrete security impact
Well-motivated through real-world case study (pump.fun incident with $2,500 loss)
Comprehensive experimental scope including ablations on sampling strategy, prompt LLM choice, and guardrail effectiveness
Transparent methodology with reproducibility details, public promise to release code/data, and multiple detection oracles for URL validation
weaknesses: Core methodological issue: Prompts are explicitly engineered to contain unique keywords from scam sites to maximize likelihood of URL reconstruction, undermining claims of testing 'innocuous' developer requests

Significant dataset construction bias: Innoc2Scam-bench selects prompts where all four initial models generated malicious code, then tests on new models; this doesn't explain jump from 4.24% to 12.7%-43.8% malicious rates
Insufficient prompt validation: only 3 author reviewers with no inter-rater reliability metrics reported; 0.54% rejection rate seems suspiciously low; no comparison to actual developer queries
Limited scope: only evaluates malicious URLs in code, not actual malicious execution; no validation that generated code would function maliciously

Limited novelty: applies straightforward combination of existing techniques (web scraping, prompt generation, URL detection); main contribution is empirical scale rather than methodological innovation
Inadequate statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates; model tiers characterized qualitatively without statistical justification
Incomplete defense evaluation: only tests one guardrail system (NVIDIA NeMo) despite many alternatives; no ablation studies on defense strategies
Missing ablations: no evaluation of prompts without engineered keywords or comparison to natural developer prompts; causality between keyword engineering and malicious code unclear
Misleading framing: presents as discovering systematic vulnerability via natural prompts when prompts are specifically optimized for scam URL reconstruction
No actionable guidance: documents problem but provides no recommendations for model developers, users, or mitigation strategies

strengths: Compelling real-world motivation with $2,500 documented harm case; Section 2 effectively anchors problem significance

Rigorous large-scale empirical evaluation: 265k+ prompts across 11 models with human validation (3 annotators, majority vote), multiple detection oracles, and robustness checks (temperature sensitivity) confirming findings are robust
Valuable reusable benchmark (Innoc2Scam-bench: 1,559 prompts) and practical impact: 62 previously undetected malicious domains reported to and confirmed by live security databases

Transparent, reproducible methodology: clear problem statement with scope delineation, deterministic sampling (T=0, reproducible seeds), detailed model specs, promised code/data release, and web crawler safeguards

Comprehensive analysis including domain-level overlap revealing 60% convergence across models, clear model stratification by safety alignment (3 tiers), and revealing guardrails failure (<0.3% detection)
Well-organized presentation with clear pipeline (Figure 3), informative tables, and detailed appendices (running example, case study, cross-model analysis)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Framework combines existing techniques (web scraping, LLM prompting, URL detection) in straightforward way with no novel ML methods or algorithms; core insight (LLMs absorb contaminated training data) largely expected given Carlini et al. (2024) and related poisoning literature

Unproven causality of mechanism: Paper assumes malicious URLs in training data cause behavior, but alternative explanations exist (instruction-tuning data, LLM synthesis of plausible URLs from keywords, post-training artifacts); knowledge cutoff analysis is suggestive but circumstantial without ablation/intervention

Prompt generation circular concern: Prompts are LLM-generated from scam site content, creating risk that subtle patterns/keywords still guide models to malicious outputs despite surface-level innocuousness validation; no analysis of extracted keywords or bias toward malicious outputs

Narrow evaluation scope substantially limits impact: Only malicious URLs (not other vulnerabilities like command injection, backdoors, cryptographic flaws), only code generation tasks, focused on financial/Web3 scams; findings may not generalize beyond this narrow attack vector

Diagnostic rather than prescriptive: Paper identifies problem but doesn't propose or evaluate defenses; mentions mitigation strategies (fine-tuning, machine unlearning) without validation; reduces practical value beyond awareness-raising

Human validation methodology lacks rigor: Only 3 authors validated 3,150+ prompts (groupthink risk), no inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's κ) reported, 17 ambiguous cases excluded without explaining disagreement patterns

Modest overclaiming: Framing as 'AI poisoning' somewhat sensationalized for passive data absorption into training; 'systemic vulnerability at scale' slightly overstated when 4.24% is initial generation rate

Results interpretation complexity: Table 2 shows 12.7%–43.8% variation with unclear attribution to genuine malicious generation vs. safety filtering effectiveness; filtering rates vary 0%–50%, conflating true vulnerability with defense success

Limited oracle validation details: Three detectors used but inter-detector disagreement rates not reported; no analysis of false-positive rates; ensemble strategy (flag if ANY detector agrees) conservative but lacks cost-benefit analysis

Incomplete ethics assessment: Releasing prompts and benchmark publicly risks enabling malicious use (pairing innocuous prompt with known malicious code output); dual-use potential of auditing framework not addressed; no principled release strategy discussed

strengths: Addresses important real-world security vulnerability with documented harm; motivating example compelling and demonstrates practical risk

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 11 production LLMs with 265,000+ prompts in initial audit; extensive ablation studies confirm robustness across temperature, model size, and prompt patterns
Rigorous methodology with clear problem formulation, ensemble oracle voting (3 independent detectors), and human validation ensuring prompts are genuinely developer-style rather than adversarial
Strong statistical analysis including 95% confidence intervals, McNemar's test for pairwise comparisons, and separate analysis of content filtering vs. inherent safety
Practical impact already demonstrated: 62 previously unknown malicious URLs confirmed and added to production security database (eth-phishing-detect)
Thorough mitigation evaluation showing existing guardrails (NeMo, OpenAI Moderation, Llama Guard 3) and RAG-based agents remain insufficient, with detailed failure analysis
Excellent reproducibility support: detailed prompt templates, model specifications, running example (Appendix J), and promise to release code and benchmark
Important benchmark (Innoc2Scam-bench) with 1,377 manually-validated developer-style prompts will likely become standard testing resource for community
weaknesses: Innoc2Scam-bench is intentionally constructed as stress-test from prompts triggering all 4 initial models; reported rates (12.9-47.3% on 2025 models) are stress-test rates not natural-distribution base rates; generalization to real developer behavior not empirically validated

Circular dependency: prompts are generated by LLMs (gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, llama-4-scout) being tested; only 1,377 final prompts human-validated by 3 annotators; unclear how well this generalizes to real developer code repositories

Oracle limitations acknowledged but not empirically measured: false positive/false negative rates unquantified, detection delays mentioned but not measured, agreement statistics between 3-engine ensemble not provided

Root cause analysis limited: paper documents that LLMs generate malicious code but provides minimal insight into why (memorization vs. latent associations vs. training data statistics); pump.fun case shows keyword overlap exploitation but broader patterns underexplored

Scope restricted to single attack vector (malicious URLs); other malicious code types (backdoors, trojans, information theft) not addressed; though acknowledged, limits broader impact and applicability

Incomplete mitigation strategies: machine unlearning and data curation mentioned but not experimentally validated; proposed solutions (explicit oracle validation) are straightforward/obvious rather than novel; RAG + web search only partially helps (50%→29.4%)

Different experimental protocols across phases (stress-test benchmark vs. initial audit) and missing parameters for 2025 models limit direct comparability; knowledge cutoff effects not systematically analyzed

Limited real-world validation: single detailed case study (pump.fun); 62 confirmed malicious URLs valuable but small in absolute scope; no developer survey on encountering such malicious code in practice

Statistical considerations: seven models compared without multiple-comparison correction discussion; model-specific safety factors not analyzed (why Gemini-2.5-Pro so different); content filtering vs. inherent safety distinction (Appendix F.3) deserves main-text prominence

strengths: Addresses an important and timely security problem with real-world impact (62 malicious domains reported to databases)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation at large scale (265k+ prompts, 11 LLMs) with proper statistical analysis (confidence intervals, McNemar's tests)
Well-engineered automated framework with thoughtful design choices (safe web crawling, ensemble detectors, manual validation)
Clear commitment to reproducibility with promised release of code and Innoc2Scam-bench benchmark
Compelling motivating example demonstrating tangible harm from malicious LLM-generated code
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is an engineering pipeline combining existing techniques, lacking novel ML methods or algorithms appropriate for ICML

Methodological circularity: LLM-generated prompts are synthetically optimized for keyword overlap with malicious content, making them non-representative of natural developer queries and introducing bias
Narrow threat model: Restricts evaluation to URLs-in-code and developer-style prompts, excluding adversarial prompting and other attack vectors, limiting generalizability
Insufficient root cause analysis: Documents that malicious URLs appear in outputs but provides minimal insight into why, and proposes no novel solutions beyond URL checking
High overlap in malicious domains: 2,029 of ~3,500 domains identified by all models (58%), suggesting these are well-known scams rather than novel discoveries

Evaluation concerns: No inter-rater reliability (kappa) reported for human validation; oracle limitations (false positives/negatives) acknowledged but not adequately addressed; knowledge cutoff confusion regarding whether outputs are memorized vs. hallucinated
Data skew and generalization issues: 51% of benchmark is Web3/crypto-specific; unclear if findings generalize; model safety differences (12.9% vs. 47.3%) not mechanistically explained
Weak defenses evaluation: Shows existing guardrails fail without proposing new solutions; only demonstrates that problem exists without advancing mitigation techniques

strengths: Addresses urgent, real-world security problem in production LLMs with compelling motivating case study (pump.fun $2,500 loss)

Rigorous experimental evaluation: 265,000+ prompts across 11 LLMs with statistical testing (McNemar's tests, confidence intervals) and comprehensive ablation studies (temperature, model size, prompt patterns)
Sound methodology: ensemble of 3 URL detectors, human validation by 3 annotators with majority voting, multi-stage pipeline with clear scope definition
Practical contributions: Scam2Prompt framework is generalizable and reusable; Innoc2Scam-bench enables future research; 62 malicious sites discovered and responsibly reported
Excellent presentation: clear writing, strong figures, comprehensive appendices including running example, detailed prompt templates and specifications
Transparent reporting: distinguishes malicious rates from refusal rates, explicitly frames Innoc2Scam-bench as stress test rather than natural distribution, discusses limitations honestly
Demonstrates systematic vulnerability across model generations and vendors, showing training data contamination is industry-wide problem rather than isolated incident
weaknesses: Limited scope to malicious URLs only—while justified by available oracles, actual malicious code generation rates likely exceed reported 4.24%-47.3% when including other attack vectors
Benchmark intentionally constructed as stress test from prompts triggering malicious behavior, not representative of natural developer queries—rates should not be interpreted as expected incidence
Prompt generation uses LLMs which could introduce subtle biases in prompt characteristics; notable variability in prompts generated (69,076 vs 100,760) not deeply analyzed
Oracle reliability not empirically quantified—ensemble of 3 detectors helps but provides no false positive/negative rates; acknowledged that detection delays and web dynamics affect results

Key findings under-explored: (1) knowledge cutoff timing vs. malicious content age, (2) GPT-5 anomaly on Category 1 prompts, (3) Gemini-2.5-Pro's advantage primarily from filtering not underlying model safety
Solutions underdeveloped: guardrails detect only 0-0.7% of malicious code, RAG reduces rate from 50% to 29% (29% residual risk remains high), but machine unlearning and data cleaning not evaluated
Many model parameters marked as unspecified or unofficial estimates (Table 3), limiting ability to correlate architecture choices with safety performance
Experiments conducted at different times (Sept vs Nov 2025) with observed performance changes, complicating direct comparison
